Check it out ! “ coincidence ,” by K Bahr on Flickr “A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed.“ Dear friend of TAoN Suzanne M sent me a link the other day to a deep-dive article about coincidences . I’d never given this subject much thought, but it turned out to be pretty interesting. And as Suzanne detected, there was a noticing/attention angle that I couldn’t help dwelling on. A coincidence, after all, has to be noticed. If I walk past a childhood friend I haven’t seen in 20 years in some airport where neither of us lives, one of us has to notice the other for the coincidence to “count,” as it were. In some ways, “ the amazing thing is not that these things occur, it’s that we notice them, ” according to David Spiegelhalter, a professor at the University of Cambridge who studies such things, as quoted in Julie Beck’s’ Atlantic article. You could say that being more attentive leads to registering more coincidences. Spiegelhalter, the article notes, has a website where people can submit their coincidence experiences, and claims to have collected something like 5,000 of them. The most common form is “ finding a link with someone you meet .” Obviously, this suggests that people who are looking for connections — who are open, curious, attentive to others — are more likely to find unexpected ones. “Coincidences never happen to me at all, because I never notice anything,” Spiegelhalter says (somewhat jokingly). “I never talk to anybody on trains. If I’m with a stranger, I don’t try to find a connection with them … .” I admit it never really occurred to me that there could be coincidence-friendly types . But Beck also cites another researcher who has found that certain personality traits are linked to experiencing more coincidences—people who describe themselves as religious or spiritual, people who are self-referential (or likely to relate information from the external world back to themselves), and people who are high in meaning-seeking are all coincidence-prone. The article goes on to explore everything from Jung’s idea of synchronicity to popular notions of the paranormal. Possibly the opposite of missing coincidences is reading too much meaning into mere chance occurrences that look like something more. The world shapes our attention, but sometimes attention shapes our world — for better or worse! That said, I’m attracted to this idea that “finding a link with someone you meet” is the most-reported form of coincidence. It’s a nice frame for chatting with someone new: Be curious, be open — and look for a happy coincidence or two. Leave a comment Thank you Suzanne! Noticing is about other people, too. title: Wild, As In Harmonious
description: * Reminder: The Savor of the Month theme for September is STRIPES. Details here ; Supporters can share their findings in the thread here . So many great contributions! Check it out ! “You need to go out into the world and look.” If you pay attention to the idea of paying attention, you have no doubt encountered the words of Mary Oliver, from her poems, essays, interviews. Oliver attracted fans ranging from John Waters to Oprah, from Stephen Colbert to Lucy Dacus. In The Art of Noticing book, I quoted from her poem “ Sometimes ”: Instructions for living a life: Pay attention. Be astonished. Tell about it. But the truth is, I didn’t really know much about Oliver’s life, and even my familiarity with her work was pretty thin. So I was very excited to see the new documentary about her, Mary Oliver: Saved By the Beauty of the World, via the PBS series American Masters. You can watch on the PBS site , or on YouTube . I recommend it! The documentary covers Oliver’s career as well her personal life, traumas included. (The title borrows from her line: “I got saved by poetry, and I got saved by the beauty of the world.”) I won’t attempt to summarize the whole thing, but I’ll share some of of the TAoN- relevant highlights. Oliver grew up in Ohio, an outsider drawn mostly to the natural world and “dead poets.” She preferred noticing to being noticed. Later, in her 20s, she learned from the intensity with which her partner, photographer Molly Malone Cook, interacted with others. Another of her familiar quotations: “ Attention without feeling … is only a report. ” Oliver and Cook lived in Provincetown, where Oliver continued her practice, attentive and poetic, walking the same paths to discover what she missed before. In time, she won major awards, and a significant audience, but to some extent the literary establishment pigeonholed her as someone who basically just went for walks and wrote about it. One person in the documentary calls her an icon of the hermit life. But that’s not the whole story. “You need to go out into the world and look,” the poet Mark Doty says in the documentary, and that’s exactly what Oliver was doing — even if it was in the nearby woods. Her appreciation of the natural world was no retreat. It was the opposite. “ Attention is the beginning of devotion, ” as she (famously) wrote in the title essay of her collection Upstream . This is perhaps her central lesson for those of us who care to go out into the world land look. “You can get ecstatic over a box of matches,” she remarks in one interview clip. And in other she makes the point I love the most: “If you love something, you give it a lot of attention. And if you give something a lot of attention, you very often learn to love it.” Yet another widely quoted Oliver line is her poetic question : “ what is it you plan to do with your one wild and precious life? ” Her own life might not sound “wild” in the way we commonly use that word. But if you don’t have time for the whole documentary, check out the clip below discussing her poem “ Wild Geese ” — and ultimately pointing out that wild can also mean natural, harmonious. title: Default Bias: Who chose your settings?
description: When a choice arrives with one option already set, most people leave it in place, regardless of whether it reflects their actual preference. The friction of changing something, combined with the implicit signal that the pre-set option is normal or recommended, produces consistent gravity toward the status quo. The mechanism runs through several channels at once. Loss aversion makes changing a default feel like risking something already owned. Implied endorsement suggests the default is a reasonable choice, so selecting it requires less justification. And the cognitive cost of evaluating alternatives encourages people to accept the existing state. These forces compound, especially in low-stakes or unfamiliar decisions where people lack strong preferences to override them. Default bias appears across organ donation programs, retirement savings enrollment, privacy settings, and software configuration. In each case, the same population of people produces dramatically different outcomes depending on which option requires action and which requires inaction. The default does not just simplify the interface. It determines the outcome for a large share of users. In design A user opens a new account and immediately lands in a signup flow. Before they have formed any preferences, the product has already decided: marketing emails are on, data sharing is enabled, notifications fire at full volume. The user clicks through, and the defaults stay. Default bias means the designer’s pre-set choices become most users’ permanent choices, whether or not those choices were made with the user’s benefit in mind. This places significant weight on the moment a default is chosen. Every pre-selected option is effectively a policy decision applied to the full user base. Designers who understand this use defaults to serve the majority, while keeping alternatives reachable. Those who ignore it discover that their defaults reflect internal convenience or business incentives rather than user needs. Applications in digital products Set the default communication preference to the least intrusive option, then let users escalate: email digests before individual notifications, not the reverse. When offering a free-to-paid upgrade, pre-select the plan that fits the user’s current usage, not the highest-tier plan, so the default reflects their situation. Place the destructive or irreversible action as the non-default: require an affirmative click to delete, unsubscribe, or share data, rather than treating those as pre-selected states. In onboarding forms, default empty fields to blank rather than placeholder values that users might submit without reading. On privacy and data settings, default to the most private configuration and present expansion as a deliberate user choice, not a correction of a setting they already “agreed to.” When a setting has a best-fit value for most users, pre-select it with a visible label like “Recommended” so the default carries transparent reasoning rather than hidden authority. Industry examples Countries with automatic organ donation enrollment see consent rates above 90%. Countries that require a positive registration act see rates below 20%. Same populations, different defaults. Thaler and Benartzi documented a similar pattern in 401(k) enrollment in 2003. Companies that switched retirement plans to automatic enrollment saw participation jump from around 50% to over 90%. Employees could still remove themselves. Most did not. Microsoft pre-selected telemetry and automatic update settings in Windows 10 that collected substantial user data. Changing them required navigating several menus. Few users did. Google enabled AI-assisted email completion in Gmail by default for all users. Adoption was high not because users chose it, but because disabling it required a deliberate action most skipped. Apple’s App Tracking Transparency, released in 2021, shifted ad tracking from an on-by-default state to an explicit prompt. Consent rates dropped from an estimated 70% to under 30%. No one changes what they don’t notice Changing a default requires two things most people avoid at the same time: forming a preference and acting on it. The pre-set option eliminates both requirements. People accept it without deliberating, often without noticing the choice was made. This is not a failure of attention, rather a rational response to cognitive load . When a decision is low-salience and the default seems reasonable, the cost of evaluating alternatives outweighs the benefit. The designer who sets the default has, in effect, already made the decision for the majority. This is why defaults carry ethical weight. A designer can claim to offer choice while structuring the choice so that most users never exercise it. Defaults are most powerful in one-time setup flows, where users move quickly and rarely return to revisit. Designers who want users to engage with settings should surface them at the moment of relevance, not bury them in preferences menus users open once and forget. Choosing the default is unavoidable. There is no neutral pre-selection. Every product that ships with a setting in place has already made a choice about whose interests that setting serves. Further reading The Power of Defaults — Jakob Nielsen, Nielsen Norman Group (2005) Defaults — The Decision Lab Status Quo Bias — The Decision Lab Choice Architecture 2.0: How People Interpret and Make Sense of Nudges — Job Krijnen, Behavioral Scientist (2018) Defaults Are Not the Same by Default — Jachimowicz, Duncan, Weber, and Johnson, Behavioral Scientist (2019) You just read why the pre-set option wins. So here’s one I’ve set for you: The reference designers keep open. Default Bias is 1 of 106 principles in Psychology of Design; the complete reference behind this newsletter. What attention does. How trust forms. Why habits stick. Each one written the way you just read this one: the mechanism, where it shows up, and how to use it. title: “Know your ‘why’ behind what you want to prove”
description: Achieving ‘success’ in creative education is interesting when it comes to transitioning into a workplace environment, because it’s not one-to-one comparable.
